title: 第八章　继续奋斗的冲动

children: 斯大林统治的岁月是20世纪最暴力的章节之一。共产主义政权粉碎了无数生命，造成的痛苦规模至今尚未完全披露。在苏联档案开放后大量挖掘出的斯大林时代的个人日记，以深刻的细节记录了政权的暴力行为如何进入苏联公民的生活，往往产生灾难性的后果。然而，同样的许多日记也流露出在大规模镇压之下强烈表达自我、实现自我的愿望。它们回响着作者参与革命思维和行动潮流的渴望，而这种潮流对他人以及对一些日记作者本人都带有破坏性的力量。在这些个人记录的创作中，自我表达与恐怖的结合对当代西方读者来说是极不协调的，需要解释。

The years of Stalin’s rule stand out as one of the most violent chapters of the twentieth century. The Communist regime shattered countless lives and caused suffering on a scale that has still not been fully revealed. Personal diaries from the Stalin era, unearthed in great numbers after the opening of the Soviet archives, document in poignant detail how the regime’s violent practices entered the lives of Soviet citizens, often with catastrophic effects. Yet many of the same diaries resonate with a striking urge for expression and self-realization amid conditions of massive repression. They reverberate with their authors’ desire to be involved in the very revolutionary currents of thinking and acting that carried such destructive power for others and for some of the diarists themselves. The association of self-expression and terror in the making of these personal records is jarring to the contemporary Western reader, and it requires explanation.

对斯大林时代日记的调查揭示了共产主义意识形态对自我的吸引力。布尔什维克活动家呼吁所有苏联民众采纳革命转型的议程，并在这一过程中实现个人的转变。融入革命共同体、帮助实现历史规律，意味着有望获得智识、道德和审美上的满足。许多日记作者将自己与革命政治挂钩，以此作为获得个人声音的一种方式，他们也称之为自己的“人格”、“传记”或“世界观”。这种声音在与个人先前无组织、“被动”或自私的存在的批判性交锋中形成，目的是塑造一个更有社会价值、更不自私且更宏大的自我。因此，加入革命可能源于一种自我表达的冲动，而不是像一些评论家所声称的那样源于一种自我抹除的冲动。

An investigation of Stalin-era diaries reveals the appeal of Communist ideology to the self. Bolshevik activists called upon all members of the Soviet population to adopt the agenda of revolutionary transformation and become personally transformed in the process. To belong to the revolutionary community and to help carry out the laws of history promised intellectual, moral, and aesthetic fulfillment. Many diarists aligned themselves with revolutionary politics as a way to acquire a personal voice, which they alternatively referred to as their “personality,” “biography,” or “worldview.” This voice took shape in critical engagement with an individual’s previous disorganized, “passive,” or selfish existence, for the purpose of sculpting a more socially valuable, less selfish, and enlarged self. Joining the revolution could thus spring from a self-expressive urge and not, as some commentators have claimed, from an impulse toward self-effacement.

虽然大量的日记作者表现出对自我修养和自我转型的关注，但关于自我的意识形态语言是高度多样化的。然而，这些记录中的许多可以根据共同的主题和20世纪20年代及30年代期间特定的时刻进行归类，当时对自我表达的愿望似乎尤为强烈。第一组日记是由“阶级异己分子”或“阶级敌人”撰写的，他们大多出身知识分子家庭，在20世纪20年代末和30年代初正如火如荼进行的推翻“旧世界”的共产主义运动背景下，寻求拆解他们的“资产阶级人格”。另一组日记描述了学习、获取文化和人格形成的过程。这些日记大多由出身下层的年轻人记录，于30年代初开始出现，是在新兴的“社会主义文明”背景下撰写的。最后是共产主义日记，它揭示了与党内清洗运动相关的自我表达的急剧上升，在大清洗时期达到顶点。

While a large number of diarists evinced a preoccupation with self-cultivation and self-transformation, the ideological language of self was highly variegated. Yet many of these records can be grouped according to shared themes and particular moments during the period of the 1920s and 1930s, when the desire for self-expression seemed to be particularly pronounced. Diaries in a first group were written by “class aliens” or “class enemies,” most of them of intelligentsia pedigree, who sought to dismantle their “bourgeois personalities” in the context of the Communist campaign to bring down the “old world,” which was in full swing in the late 1920s and early 1930s. Another set of diaries described processes of learning, acquisition of culture, and personality formation. Kept mostly by young people of lower-class origins, these began to appear in the early 1930s and were written against the background of an emerging “socialist civilization.” Finally there was the Communist diary, which revealed a dramatic rise in self-expression in connection with internal party purge campaigns, culminating in the years of the Great Purges.

“如果你想一想，有多少生命正在你身边度过，”年轻教师薇拉·帕夫洛娃（Vera Pavlova）在1932年的日记中写道，“有的长，有的短，有的充实，有的荒芜，有的灿烂，有的沉闷，有的幸福，有的不幸。有多少不同的人——创造性的和破坏性的，那些建设的人，那些独自奋斗的人，以及那些与集体共同奋斗的人，那些以某种方式成为社会生活共同大厦一部分的人，那些像沙粒一样的人，历史无形地在它的史册上铭刻下了他们。”帕夫洛娃被她周围人态度的差异所震撼；然而更令人震撼的是她用来理解生活的范畴。那是建设与破坏、集体主义与个人主义、灿烂表现与沉闷存在的二元对立范畴，这些范畴是新兴社会主义时代的特征。

“If you think about it, how many lives are being lived around you,” the young teacher Vera Pavlova noted in her diary in 1932, “lives long and short, full and barren, bright and dull, happy and unhappy. How many different people—creative and destructive, those who build, those who struggle alone and those who do so with the collective, people who in one way or another become part of the common edifice of the life of society, people like grains of sand, whom history invisibly inscribes on its pages.” Pavlova was struck by the variations in the attitudes of the people around her; yet more striking are the categories she employed to make sense of life. These were the Manichean categories of construction and destruction, collectivism and individualism, bright expression and dull existence, which characterized the emerging socialist age.

帕夫洛娃相信，所有这些不同的、甚至是截然相反的生命，都以符合历史规律的方式展开。这一思想——即历史提供了一个人生命的终极标准，一个人的生命越是服务于社会的需要，就越具有表现力，因此也就越具有历史价值——超出了帕夫洛娃个人的案例。它是斯大林时代更普遍的自我定义的构成要素，特别是在战前“社会主义建设”阶段。正是这种在更大的集体中并为历史行动服务的自我表达导向，构成了社会主义主体性。由于其共同的力量和历史意义，这种生活承诺了真实性和深刻的意义，并被强烈地渴望。它与生活在集体或历史流动之外的生活形成对比。就像日记作者渴望分享集体的生活一样，他们害怕被驱逐出这个宇宙后所带来的意义真空。一些人谈到他们害怕变成一个社会不需要的“多余人”；另一些人则把自己比作契诃夫戏剧中无助的角色，被动地看着生活和历史向前发展，逐渐超出他们日益狭窄的个人视野。在一个人的公共价值和自尊都主要取决于其“对社会的有用程度”的时代，他们奋斗着不让自己成为多余的人。在这场奋斗中，日记作者用高度具象化的术语构建了他们对归属的希望以及对不归属的恐惧。他们把集体描述为一个活的有机体，依附于它便赋予了个人力量、意义和活力。反之，无力或不愿与集体步调一致则会产生致残或瘫痪的效果，因为日记作者感到自己与那脉动着的、热情的、永远年轻的革命躯体隔绝了。

Pavlova believed that all these different, indeed contrasting, lives unfolded in historically lawful fashion. This idea—that history furnished the ultimate standard of a person’s life and that the more a person’s life served the needs of society and the more expressive it therefore was, the more historically valuable it was—goes beyond Pavlova’s personal case. It was constitutive of self-definition more generally in the Stalin years, particularly during the prewar phase of “socialist construction.” It is this orientation toward self-expression within a larger collective and in the service of historical action that constituted socialist subjectivity. On account of its communal strength and historical significance, this life promised authenticity and profound meaning, and it was intensely desired. It was contrasted to a life lived outside the collective or the flow of history. As much as diarists longed to partake in the life of the collective, they feared the void of meaning that expulsion from this universe entailed. Some spoke of their fear of turning into a “superfluous person,” not needed by society; others compared themselves to the helpless characters of Chekhov’s plays, who passively watched as life and history progressed beyond their waning personal horizons. They struggled not to be superfluous in an age when both their public worth and their self-esteem were determined above all by the extent of their “usefulness to society.” In this struggle, diarists framed their hopes for belonging as well as their fears of not belonging in highly corporeal terms. They described the collective as a living organism, adherence to which imparted personal power, meaning, and vitality. In turn an inability or unwillingness to march in step with the collective could have crippling or paralyzing effects, as diarists felt cut off from the pulsating, enthusiastic, forever young revolutionary body.

在几部日记中反复出现的一个意象是，广播为那些被“生命总流”撇下的孤独个体提供了与社会的替代性联系。作为苏联节日游行庆典声音的传播者，或者播报苏联人民最新英雄事迹的晚间新闻的传播者，广播成了集体的化身。其广播节目越是让孤独的听众充满热情，他们就越是描述出一种在苏联历史宇宙中的归属感。然而，孤独的日记作者除了通过广播的沙沙杂音或在日记中记录思想之外，无法创造出联系感，这种景象本身就唤起了一种隔绝和绝望，这是对那些被热烈描述的归属情景的一种心照不宣的反面。

A recurrent image in several diaries is that of the radio providing a surrogate connection to society for lonely individuals bypassed by the “general stream of life.” As a transmitter of the festive sounds of Soviet holiday parades, or of the evening news with its proclamations of the Soviet people’s most recent exploits, the radio became an embodiment of the collective. The more its broadcasts infused solitary listeners with enthusiasm, the more they described a sense of belonging in the Soviet historical universe. Yet the very picture of the lonely diarist, unable to create a feeling of connection other than through the crackling sounds of the radio or the recording of his thoughts in a diary, evokes isolation and despair, the unstated obverse to intensely described scenarios of belonging.

社会主义主体性最好不要被理解为一个固定的实体，某种可以一劳永逸拥有的东西，而应被理解为一种通过将自我从狭隘、卑微的关怀提升到历史参与和行动的高级层面而达到的心理状态。要使这种倾向持久，就需要持续努力地在世界中定位自己。并非那个时代的每一部日记都等量地展示了社会主义主体性的运作，更少有日记能揭示其定义特征的总和。但这种对自我表达、集体行动和历史目标的三重估价，构成了苏联社会中自我定义的基本立场。这种理想的人格形式在缺乏对自主和私人价值的积极评价这一意义上，显然是非自由主义的。值得注意的是，不仅是共产主义意识形态家，那些具有批判精神的苏联知识分子也对“资产阶级”关于个人主义创造力和特殊性的主张表示蔑视。

Socialist subjectivity is best understood not as a fixed entity, something one could possess once and for all, but as a state of mind that was attained in the very act of raising the self above its petty, parochial concerns onto the higher plane of historical engagement and action. To be lasting, this disposition required an ongoing effort to situate oneself in the world. Not every diary from this age shows the workings of socialist subjectivity in equal measure, and even fewer reveal the sum of its defining traits. But this disposition with its triple valuation of self-expression, collective action, and historical purpose mapped the default position for self-definition in the Soviet realm. This ideal form of personhood was markedly illiberal in the sense that it lacked a positive evaluation of autonomy and private values. Significantly, not only Communist ideologues but also critically minded Soviet intellectuals expressed disdain for “bourgeois” claims to individualist creativity and exceptionalism.

布尔什维克活动家成功地宣传了通过追随革命实现个人成长的紧迫性，因为这种思维深深植根于俄罗斯的历史过去。在1917年革命之前的近一个世纪里，自我完善、社会活动和与历史共鸣的自我表达的道德责任，一直是俄罗斯思想生活和政治生活的基石。当斯大林时代的日记作者努力使自己与历史保持一致并实现一种有历史根基的自我概念时，他们的行为与自19世纪初以来几代受教育的俄罗斯人惊人地一致。表现出这样的行为正是区分俄罗斯知识分子成员的标志。

Bolshevik activists were successful in propagating the urgency of individual growth through adherence to the revolution because such thinking was rooted in Russia’s historical past. The moral duties of self-improvement, social activism, and self-expression in concert with history were a staple of Russian intellectual and political life for almost a century before the revolution of 1917. As Stalin-era diarists worked to align themselves with history and to achieve a historically grounded notion of selfhood, they acted in striking consistency with generations of educated Russians since the early nineteenth century. To behave in such ways was what distinguished a member of the Russian intelligentsia.

知识分子的创始一代是一小群受过高等教育的年轻俄罗斯人，他们聚集在莫斯科和圣彼得堡的文学哲学沙龙中，因对俄罗斯“落后”的社会和政治条件的深刻不满以及改变这些条件的道德承诺而团结在一起。他们在德国唯心主义中找到了迅速而确定的转型工具，特别是黑格尔关于意识通过历史展开的哲学，他们研究这些思想不仅是作为一套观念，而且是作为个人、社会和政治生活的指南。黑格尔的教导赋予了他们对历史普遍规律存在的信仰，这同样适用于俄罗斯，并在暗淡的现状中提供了希望。尽管俄罗斯目前落后于更先进的西方，但它可以通过那些了解历史规律并献身于为国家利益应用这些规律的“有意识”个人的集中努力而赶上来。

The founding generation of the intelligentsia, a small group of highly educated young Russians, convened in literary-philosophical salons in Moscow and St. Petersburg, united by a profound disaffection with Russia’s “backward” social and political conditions and a moral commitment to changing them. They found an instrument of swift and certain transformation in German idealism, notably Hegel’s philosophy of consciousness unfolding through history, which they studied not just as a set of ideas, but as a guide to personal, social, and political life. Hegel’s teachings imparted to them a belief in the existence of universal laws of history, which also applied to Russia and provided hope amid a bleak present. Though Russia was currently lagging behind the more advanced West, it could catch up by means of the concentrated efforts of “conscious” individuals, who knew the laws of history and devoted their lives to applying them for the country’s benefit.

事实上，这些年轻人中的大多数出生在特权阶层，这在他们看来转化为一种道德义务，即使他们蒙昧的农民同胞——后来也包括工人群众——从奴隶般的人变成真正的人，然后这些人会挺身反抗压迫并帮助推动俄罗斯前进。然而，对于知识分子来说，首要的职责是自我反思：在自己身上培养一种致力于社会和政治变革的倾向；坚持认为一个人的生命必须为历史服务的观念。当知识分子谈论“人格”（lichnost'）的理想时，他们心中所想的正是这种倾向，他们将其定义为一种具有超个人本质的伦理理想——一种历史导向，以及对集体目标而非个人主义目标的投入，以服务于达到更美好的未来。

The fact that most of these young people had been born into positions of privilege translated for them into a moral obligation to raise their countrymen, the benighted peasant—and, later, worker—masses, from slavelike creatures to the stature of true human beings, who would then rise up against oppression and help move Russia forward. The primary duty for the intelligent, however, was self-reflective: to cultivate in oneself a disposition toward social and political change; to remain obligated to the idea that one’s life had to serve history. It was this disposition that members of the intelligentsia had in mind when they spoke of the ideal of “personality” (lichnost’), which they defined as an ethical ideal with a transpersonal essence—a historical orientation and an investment in collective rather than individualistic aims, in the service of reaching the better future.

这些职责虽然苛刻，但也带来了显著的回报。相信自己的思想和行为具有历史意义，为他们提供了沙皇俄国的官方体制所无法提供的意义：这些“多余的人”因持批判观点而被排除在体制之外。历史提供了一个逃离难以忍受的现状的出口，以及一个可以让他们安身立命的广阔未来。在他们中的一些人看来，那个未来看起来极为吉祥。由于注视着决定历史发展步伐的西方，他们预感到俄罗斯人格的紧密培养终有一天会促使这个“年轻”国家超越“古老”的西方，他们认为西方正被退化的、追求私利的“资产阶级”价值观所拖累。

These responsibilities, while demanding, also carried significant rewards. The belief that one’s thoughts and actions had historical relevance provided meaning where none was to be found in the official structures of tsarist Russia, from which these “superfluous people” saw themselves barred on account of their critical opinions. History offered an escape from the unbearable present, and a rich future expanse in which they could make themselves at home. To some of them, that future looked most auspicious. With an eye to the West, which dictated the pace of historical development, they sensed that intense cultivation of personality in Russia would one day propel this “young” nation past the “old” West, which they saw as weighed down by degenerative, self-seeking “bourgeois” values.

知识分子发展其关于历史变革思想的主要舞台是文学。鉴于专制统治下的政治审查环境，正是在表面的非政治文学领域，在小说、评论文章和文学自传中，“新人”的属性才得以描绘和讨论。同样地，阅读这些作品为知识分子成员提供了一面镜子，供其凝视以便实现转型。因此，生活与艺术之间建立起了一种强烈的互惠关系，知识分子典范式的生活成为了文学角色的原型，读者反过来又效仿这些角色。这些极具渗透性的边界，链接而非分割了生活与文本，并将贯穿20世纪的大部分时间，它们是斯大林时代日记的一个显著特征。

列宁和其他布尔什维克遵循着通过文学传达的使命生活，即为历史服务，过一种典范的生活。他们模仿关于新人的开创性读物来塑造自己的态度，并反过来根据他们不断发展的关于必要历史行动的信念，宣扬行为模式。列宁关于由职业革命家组成的新型政党的论著《怎么办？》（What Is to Be Done?, 1902）读起来也像是一本培养人格的手册。一个紧密结合的政党环境要培育出具有极度奉献精神和坚定意志的同志，这些男女拥有如此高的意识和铁的意志，以至于他们能够引领落后的俄罗斯进入世界革命的旋风。

The main arena in which the intelligentsia developed its ideas about historical change was literature. Given the conditions of political censorship under autocratic rule, it was in the ostensibly nonpolitical literary sphere, in novels, critical essays, and literary autobiographies, that the properties of the “new man” were sketched out and discussed. By the same token, the reading of these works provided members of the intelligentsia with a mirror into which to gaze so as to be transformed. Thus a relationship of intense reciprocity between life and art took hold, where the intellectual’s exemplary life served as a model for a literary character on whom readers in turn patterned themselves. These highly porous boundaries, linking, rather than separating, life and text, would persist through much of the twentieth century, and they are a remarkable feature of Stalin-era diaries.

Lenin and other Bolsheviks lived by the mandate, relayed through literature, to lead a model life in the service of history. They patterned their attitudes on seminal readings about the new man, and in turn they preached models of behavior in correspondence with their evolving convictions about necessary historical action. Lenin’s treatise on a new type of political party of professional revolutionaries, What Is to Be Done? (1902), also reads as a manual of personality cultivation. A tightly knit party milieu was to rear comrades of the utmost dedication and steadfastness, men and women who commanded such consciousness and iron willpower that they were capable of ushering backward Russia into the whirlwind of world revolution.
在掌权之后，布尔什维克系统地压制了非布尔什维克知识分子提出的竞争性历史变革方案。在党内，一个平行的过程也在进行，即压制“反对派”的声音，并强加一条日益等同于斯大林个人意志的“总路线”（General Line）。激进知识分子的精神在共产党内部起作用，但在苏联国家建立的机构和发起的运动中找到了更广泛的应用。从成立之初，苏联政府就致力于开展全面的扫盲和教育运动，事实证明这些运动取得了惊人的成功。

After coming to power, the Bolsheviks systematically suppressed competing scenarios of historical change propounded by non-Bolshevik members of the intelligentsia. Inside the party, a parallel process went on, of shutting off “oppositional” voices and imposing a “General Line” that increasingly became identified with Stalin’s personal will. The spirit of the radical intelligentsia was at work within the Communist party, but it found even broader application in institutions and campaigns set up by the Soviet state. From the first days of its existence the Soviet government engaged in comprehensive literacy and education campaigns, which proved astoundingly successful.

随着其苏维埃化，知识分子的风气发生了转变。它从影响俄罗斯受教育社会的一个小阶层，扩散成为一种通过苏联国家机构体制宣传的普遍理想。虽然这一理想在解释上变得更加狭隘，在性格上变得更加威权，但其轮廓依然清晰可辨：它表现为一种现在延伸到每个苏联公民身上的指令，即过一种意识形态统一的、“有意识”的生活，致力于“社会”的需求，并最终致力于历史的进步。从1917年前延续到苏联时期的承诺，在齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅（Zinaida Denisevskaya）的日记中得到了体现，她一生都认同知识分子的启蒙使命。但知识分子的价值观也塑造了在20世纪20年代和30年代成长的农民出身的工人的自我构想。列昂尼德·波特姆金（Leonid Potemkin）利用他的日记将他把自己改造为社会主义人格的努力系统化。斯捷潘·波德卢布内（Stepan Podlubny）的努力虽然受到其被压抑的过去这一负担的阻碍，但他的人格养成（Bildung）之路显示了类似的抱负。

As it was Sovietized, the intelligentsia ethos became transformed. From affecting a small layer of Russia’s educated society, it spread to become a universal ideal that was propounded through the institutional apparatus of the Soviet state. While the ideal became narrower in interpretation and more authoritarian in character, its contours remained distinctly present: in the form of a mandate, now extended to every Soviet citizen, to lead an ideologically integrated, “conscious” life, devoted to the needs of “society,” and ultimately to the progression of history. The intricate ways in which commitments carried over from before 1917 into the Soviet period are illustrated in the diary of Zinaida Denisevskaya, who identified with the enlightening mission of the in-telligentsia throughout her life. But intelligentsia values also shaped the self-conceptions of peasant workers who grew up in the 1920s and 1930s. Leonid Potemkin used his diary to systematize his efforts to re-make himself into a socialist personality. Stepan Podlubny’s efforts were hampered by the burden of his suppressed past, but his road to Bildung revealed a similar aspiration.
问题仍然在于，如何将这些关于强烈内省和追求的叙事与苏联政权施加的心理和身体方面的政治压力联系起来。鉴于共产主义国家要求热切参与“社会主义建设”，它监控公民思想的决心，以及它对哪怕是最轻微的反对行为迹象的迫害，人们可能会怀疑，日记作者主要是写给内务人民委员部看，并努力塑造一个自己是苏维埃政权狂热拥护者的形象，这背离了他们真实的信念和信仰。

The question remains how to situate these narratives of intense in-trospection and striving in relation to the political pressures, psychological and physical, applied by the Soviet regime. In view of the Communist state’s demands for enthusiastic participation in the “building of socialism,” its determination to police the thought of its citizens, and its persecution of even the slightest indications of oppositional behavior, it may be suspected that diarists wrote primarily for the eyes of the NKVD and worked hard to present an image of themselves as ardent supporters of Soviet power, in departure from their actual convictions and beliefs.

齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅写了三十多年的日记，跨越了1917年和十年后斯大林工业革命的双重门槛。在整个这一时期，她的自我理解不断发展，但没有突然的中断或语气的转变；它始终如一地展开，并遵循其内在逻辑。德尼谢夫斯卡娅从未突然改变方向，从未从真诚和自我披露的风格转向某种为外部读者准备的更有算计的自我呈现方式。其他日记覆盖的时间跨度较短，但它们的开头都延伸到了斯大林镇压之前的时期。它们在主题焦点和自我表达风格上也是一致的。亚历山大·阿菲诺格诺夫早在1932年就探讨了他的艺术和个人危机，但直到1937年在政权的巨大压力下，他才认真地面对自己的“退化”。当列昂尼德·波特姆金开始记日记时，他致力于自我教育，这一计划他在随后的几年里有系统地执行。他在1936年停止记日记，因为日记不再能帮助他追求更好的自我。相反，他转向与同龄人直接交流，包括他与伊拉·日尔科娃（Ira Zhirkova）的大量通信。斯捷潘·波德卢布内的情况更复杂，因为他自觉地过着双重生活，假装是工人，同时知道自己来自不同的阶级。然而，他的日记声音是一致的；他的日记作为一个批判性的评论和他为双重生活寻找解决方案的过程而展开，而不是这种生活的延伸。在关于特定日记作者的四个章节中，除了日记，我还利用了其他来源——私人信件、诗歌、回忆录、照片、出版的著作和访谈。共同研究这些来源可以揭示比日记本身所能传达的更复杂的个人主体性概念；然而，它们并没有使日记的记述失效或与之矛盾。在日记内外的显著特征是，一种普遍的社会监视、自我干预和自我完善的议程。

Zinaida Denisevskaya kept her diary for more than thirty years, across the double threshold of 1917 and Stalin’s industrial revolution a decade later. Throughout this period her self-understanding kept evolving, but without sudden breaks or shifts in tonality; it unfolded with consistency, and according to its own logic. Nowhere did Denisevskaya turn in her tracks, shifting from a style of sincerity and self-disclosure to a more calculated form of self-presentation intended for an outside reader. The other diaries cover shorter time spans, but their beginnings extend back to the period preceding Stalin’s repressions. They, too, are consistent in thematic focus and self-expressive style. Alexander Afinogenov addressed his artistic and personal crisis as early as in 1932, but it was only in 1937, under intense pressure from the regime, that he earnestly engaged with his “degeneration.” When Leonid Potemkin began to keep his diary, he devoted it to his self-education, a project that he pursued systematically in the following years. He gave up writing in the diary in 1936 because it no longer aided him in his quest for a better self. Instead, he turned to direct interchange with his peers, including his extensive correspondence with Ira Zhirkova. Stepan Podlubny’s case is more complicated in that he consciously led a double life, pretending to be a worker while knowing that he was from a different class. Yet his diaristic voice was consistent; his diary unfolded as a critical commentary and a search for a solution to his double life, not as its extension. In each of the four chapters about particular diarists, I have drawn on other sources in addition to the diary— private letters, poems, memoirs, photographs, published writings, and interviews. Studied in concert, they reveal a more complex notion of individual subjectivity than a diary alone can impart; yet they do not in-validate or contradict the diaristic account. What is evident both in the diaries and beyond them is a pervasive agenda of social surveillance, self-intervention, and self-perfection.

波德卢布内、德尼谢夫斯卡娅和阿菲诺格诺夫的日记中充满了个人怀疑和政治观点的表达，尤其是在政治压力加剧的时候。回想一下波德卢布内，他把日记视为存放他“反动”思想的仓库；或者阿菲诺格诺夫试图从他的共产主义生活中逃往私人存在；或者德尼谢夫斯卡娅对党的总路线有效性的怀疑。如果日记被没收，并以国家检察官不信任的目光来阅读，这些思路无疑会引发关于“退化”、“反对派情绪”或“反革命意图”的指控。因此，这类段落的存在实际上否定了那种认为这些日记主要是为了斯大林安全机构的耳目而创作的猜疑。尽管如此，仍有人可能假设，即使是这些怀疑和绝望的陈述也是针对内务人民委员部的，旨在唤起一种挣扎着的信徒的形象，他们正因为没有隐瞒怀疑而值得被信任。然而，如果将日记中长年累月维持的成百上千页内容解读为一种精心策划的姿态，那不仅是对这些文件的不公，也是对其作者的不公。这种解读无法解释斯大林时代无数的自传性文件，这些文件表明内省和自我教育是既定的文化实践。作者们竭尽全力去获取供应稀缺的纸张和笔记本；这种努力及其对记录的长期依恋表明，他们有强烈的动机去面对、钻研并解决关于自身的紧迫问题。

Podlubny’s, Denisevskaya’s, and Afinogenov’s diaries are rich in expressions of personal doubt and political opinion, especially pronounced at times when political pressures were intensifying. Recall Podlubny, who addressed his diary as a repository of his “reactionary” thoughts; or Afinogenov’s attempt to escape from his Communist life into a private existence; or Denisevskaya’s doubts about the validity of the party’s General Line. Had the diaries been confiscated and read with the distrustful eyes of a state prosecutor, these trains of thought would doubtless have given rise to charges of “degeneration,” “oppositionist moods,” or “counterrevolutionary intent.” Thus the presence of such passages effectively invalidates the suspicion that these diaries were produced primarily for the eyes and ears of the Stalinist security apparatus. Still, some might hypothesize that even these statements of doubt and despair were aimed at the NKVD, to evoke a picture of struggling believers who deserved to be trusted precisely because they did not conceal their doubts. Yet to read page after page of a diary as expression of a calculated pose, maintained for years on end, does in-justice to these documents and their authors. Such a reading cannot account for the myriad autobiographical documents from the Stalin era which indicate that introspection and self-education were established cultural practices. Authors went to great lengths to procure paper and notebooks, which were in scarce supply; this and their prolonged attachment to their records suggest that they were strongly motivated to confront, work through, and resolve pressing questions about themselves.

从这个角度来看，我所讨论的日记不仅是文本产物和被动的见证。它们也是持续不断的自我探寻和自我改变努力的物质残留，这些努力受到一种将成员定义为革命自我的文化的鼓励。关于奋斗和自我生成的日记叙述指向了日记之外的领域，超出了特定日记作者的社会形象。在表达其追求时，日记作者渴望在日记之外，在实践和持续的工作中，以一种历史行动的模式实现自我。沉浸在纯粹思想中的日记，充其量只是描述了一种替代性的历史行动。许多反思性的日记是由被排除在集体之外的人撰写的，他们转向日记以创造一种替代性的归属感。日记的反思可以进一步推动改造自我的计划，但这一计划的主要舞台在别处，即工作和积极的社会参与领域。因此，这些反思性的日记叙述引导我们的视野转向更广阔的自我构建与重建领域，这些领域渗透在苏联的社会、政治和经济景观中。

Seen in this light, the diaries I have discussed are more than textual artifacts and a form of passive testimony. They are also a material residue of sustained efforts at self-searching and self-change, efforts encouraged by a culture that defined its members in terms of revolutionary selves. Diaristic accounts of struggle and self-becoming point to a sphere beyond the diary, and beyond the social profile of a given diarist. In expressing their strivings, diarists longed to realize themselves in a mode of historical action outside their diaries, in practical and ongoing work. The diary, steeped in thought alone, described at best a form of surrogate historical action. Many self-reflective diaries were written by people who were excluded from the collective and turned to their journals to create a substitute sense of belonging. Diaristic reflection could further the project of reworking the self, but the principal arena of this project was elsewhere, in the spheres of work and active social engagement. Thus these self-reflective diary narratives direct our view to a much wider field of self-construction and reconstruction that permeated the Soviet social, political, and economic landscapes.

就像任何其他历史时期一样，只有将斯大林时代的主体置于其文化环境中，我们才能对其产生深刻的理解，这种文化环境提供了进入日记创作的言论、思想和行动范畴。如果苏联公民坚持自我修养的至高需求；如果他们声称自己把日记作为自我锤炼的实验室，并为了相互监护灵魂而与朋友交换信件，我们没有理由不相信他们的话，即使我们判定他们的议程是受误导或被蒙蔽的。对于这些作者具有定义性重要意义的自我改变指令和与历史同步的社会化自我理想，在对斯大林时期的分析评估中也需要得到承认。这种历史理解绝不意味着同情或认可历史行为者的选择。相反，目标是将我们历史主体的自我理解与我们当代的自我观念区分开来。同情会产生相反的效果：它通过将我们自己的价值观和自我概念投射到历史行为者身上，从而打破了分析的距离。我们按照我们的形象重塑那些行为者，这种形象是由个人主义和自主的自由主义理想所塑造的，而我们将那些不符合这一形象的方面相对化或丢弃。

As is true for any other historical period, we gain a deep understanding of Stalin-era subjects only by situating them in their cultural environment, which supplied the very categories of speech, thought, and action that went into the production of their diaries. If Soviet citizens insisted on a paramount need for self-cultivation; if they claimed they kept diaristic laboratories for working on their selves and exchanged letters with friends for the purpose of monitoring each other’s souls, we have no reason not to take them at their word, even if we judge their agenda to have been deluded or misguided. The imperative of self-change and the ideal of a socialized self in tune with history, which held defining importance for these authors, need to be acknowledged in analytical appraisals of the Stalin period as well. Such historical understanding in no way implies sympathizing with, or endorsing, historical actors’ choices. The goal is, on the contrary, to separate the self-understandings of our historical subjects from our contemporary conceptions of self. Sympathy has the opposite effect: it breaks down analytical distance by projecting onto historical actors our own values and notions of self. We remake those actors in our image, shaped by liberal ideals of individualism and autonomy, and we relativize or discard aspects that do not fit that image.

工程师尤利娅·皮亚特尼茨卡娅（Julia Piatnitskaya）在丈夫被捕后被苏联社会抛弃的困境令人同情。然而，很难认同她在1938年对尼古拉·布哈林（Nikolai Bukharin）是叛徒和间谍的谴责。一年前，皮亚特尼茨卡娅的丈夫曾在共产党内为布哈林辩护，对抗指责他的人，这种立场可能导致了皮亚特尼茨基（Piatnitsky）本人被捕。在读到布哈林在莫斯科公开审判中承认他策划了恐怖阴谋（这实际上是他的内务人民委员部审讯者虚构的）后，皮亚特尼茨卡娅得出了一个令我们今天感到不安的结论，即她的丈夫在为这个伪装起来的恶毒敌人辩护时犯了错。
同样地，我们也可能同情齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅，尤其是考虑到她短暂生命中频繁发生的许多灾难。

The plight of the engineer Julia Piatnitskaya, discarded from Soviet society after her husband was arrested, invites sympathy. Yet it is difficult to identify with her condemnation of Nikolai Bukharin as a traitor and spy in 1938. A year earlier Piatnitskaya’s husband had defended Bukharin against his accusers in the Communist party, and this stance had probably led to Piatnitsky’s own arrest. Reading Bukharin’s confession, at the Moscow show trial, that he had orchestrated terrorist plots (which in fact had been invented by his NKVD interrogators), Piatnitskaya came to the conclusion, disturbing to us today, that her husband had erred in defending a spiteful enemy in disguise.
We may equally sympathize with Zinaida Denisevskaya, particularly in light of the many calamities that punctuated her short life.

然而，在这种解读中，无法容纳德尼谢夫斯卡娅坚持拥抱每一个新的政治转折，视其为历史上不可避免且值得追求的行为，甚至包括最终导致她死亡的苏联阶级斗争政治。斯捷潘·波德卢布内作为一个被打上“阶级敌人”烙印的儿子的心理剧无疑会引发同情。然而，他对乌克兰饥饿农民的评论令人不寒而栗（“让他们死吧。如果他们不能保护自己免于饿死，这意味着他们意志薄弱，他们能给社会带来什么？”）。还有列昂尼德·波特姆金，他在审美上崇拜社会主义建设，但他对美丽和表现力的世界新愿景，是建立在暴力斗争、退化和腐朽的情景之上的，他不仅仅是在隐喻意义上理解这些情景。

Yet there is no place in this reading for Denisevskaya’s insistence on embracing every new political turn as historically unavoidable and desirable, even the Soviet politics of class war that ultimately killed her. Stepan Podlubny’s psychological drama as a stigmatized son of a “class enemy” is sure to invite sympathy. Yet his comments about the starving peasants in Ukraine are chilling (“Let them die. If they can’t defend themselves against death from starvation, it means that they are weak-willed, and what can they give to society?”). And then there is Leonid Potemkin, who worshipped the building of socialism in aesthetic terms, but whose vision of the new world of beauty and expression was premised on scenarios of violent struggle, degeneration, and decay, which he understood in more than just metaphorical ways.

让当代西方读者觉得这些思想模式如此具有挑战性的原因，在于它们为了自我实现而接受暴力。虽然斯大林政权对其公民采取了极端形式的暴力，但他们自己的自我理解也充满了象征性的暴力。奋斗、针对外部和内部敌人的运动，以及为了建立“新人”而消灭“旧人”，都是苏联主体性的核心组成部分。对力量、健康和美丽的普罗米修斯式颂扬，伴随着对那些被视为软弱、患病和不适应生活的人的公开蔑视。个人主体与国家行为者在革命性的净化社会空间和个人灵魂的平行轨道上保持一致，双方都将暴力视为塑造社会和自我的必要工具。历时性地跨越战争、革命和斯大林工业化的门槛来看，日记揭示了个人形式的自我投入依赖于一种暴力环境来实现其圆满。连续记录的条目显示出对自我思考的紧迫感增加，而记录中的疏漏和空白则指出向内审视的激励减少。政权在20世纪20年代末发起的针对“旧世界”的战争，引起了认同“资产阶级知识分子”的个人的大量反思；30年代的共产主义式政治审判则将处于火力线上的布尔什维克送上了内省的旅程。因此，个别日记作者将施加在他们身上的政治暴力转化为内省的催化剂。在这一过程中，许多人将外部压力转化为内部反思，将行政强制转化为心理欲望。但在这样做时，他们不断阐述自己在特定清洗或运动之前就已经存在的观点。在反思他们面临的压力时，日记作者保留了他们叙事的主创权，我们没有理由将他们纹理细密的记录归类为仅仅是“随声附和”——背诵苏联政权规定的咒语。

What renders these modes of thought so challenging to contemporary Western readers is their acceptance of violence in the service of self-realization. While the Stalinist regime practiced extreme forms of violence toward its citizens, their own self-understanding was suffused with symbolic violence as well. Struggle, campaigns against external and internal enemies, and the destruction of the Old Man in order to build the New Man were all core components of Soviet subjectivity. Promethean celebrations of strength, health, and beauty went along with open disdain for those who were considered weak, sick, and unfit for life. Individual subjects and state actors were aligned on parallel trajectories of revolutionary purification of social space and individual souls, and both regarded violence as a necessary tool to mold society and the self. Viewed diachronically across the thresholds of war, revolution, and Stalinist industrialization, diaries reveal that individual forms of self-engagement depended on an environment of violence to reach fulfillment. Entries written in daily succession suggest an increased urgency in thinking about oneself, while lapses and gaps in the record point to a reduced incentive to turn the gaze inward. The war against the “old world” launched by the regime in the late 1920s engendered much reflection on the part of individuals who identified with the “bourgeois intelligentsia”; the Communist inquisition of the 1930s sent Bolsheviks caught in the line of fire on journeys of introspection. Individual diarists thus turned the political violence applied against them into a catalyst for introspection. In the process many reworked external pressure into internal reflection, administrative coercion into psychological desire. Yet in so doing they kept elaborating views of themselves that had existed before a particular purge or campaign. While reflecting on the pressures they faced, diarists retained authorship of their narratives, and we have no reason to classify their densely textured records as instances of mere “singing along”—reciting incantations prescribed by the Soviet regime.

为了进一步实现自我转型，日记作者寻求切除并丢弃不必要的或有害的想法。将这称为“自我审查”并不完全恰当。在这些实例中，日记作者面对并加工他们尚未完全清醒的思想和身体的声音，以使他们真正的道德“自我”得以浮现。自我修养主要是一种道德追求，旨在自我完善和生存验证。相比之下，“自我审查”应仅用于指代由日记作者担心其思想或行为会受到政治惩罚而引发的个人自我压抑行为。道德塑造和政治自我审查这两个方面都出现在斯大林时代的日记中，且它们经常重叠和融合，日记作者对外部镇压的恐惧和生存自我的丧失不加区分。这种融合在一些苏联日记作者的困境中得到了深刻的表达，他们在精神危机时刻，将内务人民委员部——斯大林政治暴力的主要机构——视为其人生的最高道德权威并向它求助，恳求它干预并纠正他们错误的思想。

To further their self-transformation, diarists sought to excise and discard unnecessary or harmful thoughts. To call this “self-censorship” is not entirely appropriate. In these instances, diarists confronted and worked on the voice of their not fully conscious mind and body to enable their true moral “self” to emerge. Self-cultivation was predominantly a moral pursuit, applied for the purposes of self-improvement and existential validation. By contrast, “self-censorship” should be used only for acts of individual self-repression motivated by diarists’ fear that their thoughts or actions would be politically sanctioned. Both aspects, moral shaping and political self-censorship, figured in Stalin-era diaries, and they often overlapped and fused, with diarists making no distinction between fear of external repression and existential self-loss. This fusion is poignantly expressed in the plight of Soviet diarists who, in times of spiritual crisis, addressed the NKVD—the chief agency of Stalinist political violence—as the ultimate moral authority over their lives, pleading that it intervene and correct their errant thoughts.

对于许多斯大林时代的日记作者来说，历史提供了将自我与政治现状对齐的动力，无论那个现状显得多么压抑。知道历史的方向并加入其革命潮流，是拥有成熟自我和成为苏联社会合法成员的条件。现状可能是暗淡的，但如果它提供了一条通向未来的道路，它就变得可以忍受，甚至是非常值得的。没有人比尤利娅·皮亚特尼茨卡娅更深刻地表达了苦难与救赎之间的这种联系，她在斯大林清洗中失去了丈夫和儿子，但却无法想象放弃为斯大林体制服务的努力：“你最亲近、最亲爱的人死去了，你备受折磨，你看到四面八方都是痛苦和死亡，但你继续前行，挺直身体，你直视社会的未来——你的生命将更灿烂、更丰富，对他人更有用。你必须活在行动中，而不是沉思中，如果无法不看到旧的、黑暗的生活，那就超越它，斩断与它的联系，寻求那条快乐而光辉的道路。”
其他日记作者也描述了个人观察到的现实与政权宣传的“革命真理”之间的强烈紧张关系，但他们通过深刻的历史反思来解决这些紧张。他们倾向于将社会主义建设的成就记录为历史标志，表明历史正步入正轨并向前迈进。

For many Stalin-era diarists, history provided the impetus to align their selves with the political present, however repressive that present appeared to them. To know where history was headed and to join its revolutionary current was the condition of possessing a developed self and being a legitimate member of Soviet society. The present could be bleak, but if it offered a path toward the future, it became livable or even eminently worthwhile. No one expressed this link between suffering and salvation more poignantly than Julia Piatnitskaya, who had lost husband and son in Stalin’s purges and yet could not conceive of giving up her efforts in the service of the Stalinist state: “Your nearest and dearest perish, you’re tormented, you see on all sides suffering and death, but you walk on, standing tall, you look straight ahead to the future of society—your life will be brighter and richer, and more useful to others. You must live in action, not in contemplation, and if it becomes impossible not to see the old, dark life, then rise above it, sever yourself from it, and seek the joyful and radiant path.”

Other diarists as well described stark tensions between personally observed reality and the “revolutionary truth” propagated by the regime, but they proceeded to resolve these tensions through intense historical reflection. They tended to register achievements of socialist construction as historical markers indicating that history was on track and marching along.

他们的解释有一定的合理性：苏俄的面貌正在迅速改变；数百万下层民众正在接受教育；政权不懈宣传的理性化、纪律和科学等现代价值观，似乎正在取代根深蒂固的俄罗斯式顺从和冷漠。通过与陷入经济萧条和政治危机的资本主义西方进行对比，这种国家正在翱翔至新高度的感觉得到了进一步确认。如此理解的历史扮演了强效麻醉剂的角色。它可以赋予一个人的生命令人陶醉的意义和气势，并以此减轻在观察到的现实与规定的真理发生冲突时的痛苦。虽然亚历山大·阿菲诺格诺夫和其他艺术知识分子成员有时会哀叹他们工作中的创造性限制条件，但他们作为新世界工程师的角色给予了他们参与历史的机会，这令非社会主义世界中的艺术家角色相形见绌。

Their interpretation had some justification: the physiognomy of Soviet Russia was rapidly changing; millions of people from the lower classes were receiving education; the modern values of rationalization, discipline, and science, relentlessly preached by the regime, seemed to be superseding ingrained Russian notions of submission and apathy. The sense that the country was soaring to new heights received further confirmation by comparison with a capitalist West mired in economic depression and political crisis. History, thus understood, acted as a powerful narcotic. It could impart intoxicating meaning and sweep to a person’s life, and in so doing it could mitigate the pain of observed reality as it clashed with the mandated truth. While Alexander Afinogenov and other members of the artistic intelligentsia sometimes deplored the conditions of creative constraint in which they worked, their role as engineers of the new world rewarded them with opportunities to participate in history that dwarfed the role of the artist in the nonsocialist world.
这种关于历史有规律发展的愿景，也影响了那些批评苏联政权、拒绝接受其历史主张的人。在献身于另一种未来的过程中，这些批评者执着于一种相同的自我观念，即在革命的历史流变中实现自我。

然而，要以这种方式挑战政权，不仅需要巨大的勇气，还需要一种通过诸如“历史”、“革命”或“人民”等范畴来构建自我的能力，而这些范畴正是政权试图垄断的。从我讨论过的日记来看，斯大林政权成功地使许多批评者噤声，这不仅是通过直接的镇压手段或镇压威胁，还通过间接的手段，即社会排斥和对社会主义自我语义的控制。在政权的强大压力下，政权实行仪式性的开除方案，在将个人丢进“历史的垃圾堆”（托洛茨基语）之前，形象地将其从集体中剥离出来。许多“多余人”变成了孤独且自我怀疑的主体，变得“不被任何人需要”——考虑到他们对社会价值和历史目标的追求，这是一种可怕的命运。

Visions of a lawful progression of history also informed those who criticized the Soviet regime and refused to accept its historical claims. In devoting themselves to an alternative future, these critics clung to an identical notion of a self that realized itself in the revolutionary flow of history.

Yet to engage the regime in such terms required not only great courage but also an ability to conceptualize oneself through categories, such as “history,” “the revolution,” or “the people,” which the regime sought to monopolize. Judging from the diaries I have discussed, the Stalinist regime was successful in silencing many of its critics not only through direct repressive means or the threat thereof, but indirectly, through social ostracism and control over the semantics of socialist selfhood. Under intense pressure from the regime, which practiced ritual expulsion scenarios, graphically severing individuals from the collective body before discarding them onto the “dustbin of history” (Trotsky), many “superfluous people” turned into lonely and self-doubting subjects, “not needed by anyone”—a terrible fate given their striving for a life of social usefulness and historical purpose.

这种渴望成为一个承诺了包容一切的世界观、确定性、意义和圆满的运动的一部分的愿望，并非苏联所特有。它是二十世纪上半叶欧洲文化和政治生活不可分割的一部分，当时新兴的大众政治和技术实验与传统的资产阶级价值观背道而驰。整个欧洲的知识分子，包括乔治·索雷尔（Georges Sorel）、恩斯特·荣格尔（Ernst Jünger）和瓦尔特·本雅明（Walter Benjamin），都赞美政治暴力在道德上的救赎能量和在审美上的净化力量。战间期欧洲的艺术景观充满了审美暴力的实验，涵盖了从形式主义风格到未来主义诗歌和先锋派电影的各个领域。左翼和右翼新兴且迅速流行的激进政党相互竞争，力图实现其审美化的社会愿景，清除其中的污染或退化因素。所有这些活动家，无论其背景和政治倾向如何，都共同拥有一种要与陈腐的、“学术的”或“资产阶级的”习惯决裂的决心，并坚持认为暴力对于他们重塑世界的计划是必要的。他们都颂扬有组织的群众所具有的优越力量、美感和道德地位，这与“软弱”且“过时”的“资产阶级个人主义”时代形成了鲜明对比。
此后，这些运动的冷酷行径和纯粹的破坏力使它们在许多人眼中名声扫地，但它们所援引的统一社会实体的形象至今仍具有现实意义。这个形象对作为现代主体的我们说话，我们虽然从传统的纽带中解放了出来，却在个人生活中漂泊无依。

The longing to be part of a movement that promised an all-embracing worldview, certainty, meaning, and fulfillment was not specific to the Soviet Union. It was integral to European cultural and political life in the first half of the twentieth century, when emerging mass politics and technological experimentation militated against traditional bourgeois values. Intellectuals across Europe, including Georges Sorel, Ernst Jünger, and Walter Benjamin, extolled the morally redemptive and aesthetically purifying energy of political violence. The artistic landscapes of interwar Europe were suffused with experiments in aesthetic violence, ranging from formalist style to futurist poetry and avant-garde filmmaking. New and immediately popular radical parties on the left and the right vied with one another for the realization of aestheticized visions of society, cleansed of polluting or degenerating agents. All these activists, whatever their backgrounds and political orientations, shared a determination to break with antiquated, “academic” or “bourgeois” habits, and an insistence on violence as necessary for their project of re-creating the world. And they all heralded the superior power, beauty, and moral standing of organized masses, in contrast to the “weak” and “outdated” age of “bourgeois individualism.”

The cynical practices and the sheer destructive power of these movements have since discredited them in the eyes of many, but the image of a unified social body that they invoked carries relevance to this day. The image speaks to us as modern subjects, freed from bonds of tradition and yet cast adrift in our individual lives.

尽管这种暴力文化是当时整个欧洲的特征，但唯独在苏联发展出了一种审判式的文化，试图识别并揭露革命运动内部具有污染性的“他者”。共产主义意识形态并没有构想出一个固定的——种族化的或社会学上静态的——敌人形象，作为争取道德和审美完美的斗争对象。未来共产主义世界的成员身份取决于一个人意识的纯洁性，因此每个个人既是净化的主体，又是净化的客体。共产主义意识形态所假设的自我的可塑性可能构成重大威胁，但起初它散发出的是承诺和魅力。这种对自我的非凡诉求是苏联共产主义国家所特有的。在二十世纪其他大众动员政权——法西斯意大利和纳粹德国——中，都没有发出如此深远的号召，要求个人在加入革命的行为中改造自己。这些政权也都没有产生出在数量和反思深度上能与苏联记录相媲美的自传体文学。

Although these cultures of violence characterized Europe as a whole in this period, only in the Soviet Union did an inquisitorial culture develop that sought to identify and expose the polluting Other within the revolutionary movement. Communist ideology did not conceive of a fixed—racialized or sociologically static—image of an enemy against whom the struggle for moral and aesthetic perfection was to be waged. Membership in the future Communist world depended on the purity of one’s consciousness, and thus every individual became subject and object of purification at the same time. The malleability of the self posited by Communist ideology could pose a major threat, but at first it emanated promise and fascination. The extraordinary appeal to the self was specific to the Soviet Communist state. Neither of the other twentieth-century regimes of mass mobilization, Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, issued such a far-reaching call to individuals to transform themselves in the act of joining the revolution. And neither of those regimes produced an autobiographical literature that rivaled the Soviet record in volume and reflective depth.

苏联意识形态的主体化冲动部分源于马克思主义及其浪漫主义根源，部分源于对社会有用性的要求，这在革命前很久就一直是俄罗斯文化的基调。真正的生活意味着超越自私的追求，将生命奉献给社会和历史，从而通过个人的榜样力量和对未来不屈不挠的导向，重塑受诅咒的、落后的俄罗斯。这种倾向在苏联统治的整个时期都以极端但可辨认的形式存在着，并在斯大林时代得到了尤为强烈的体现。在后斯大林时期，其强度有所减弱。1936年，忧郁的莫斯科年轻工人、共青团员亚历山大·乌里扬诺夫（Alexander Ulianov）在两个女孩之间纠结不已，他最终宣称，他献身于生命中真正的挚爱——“亲爱的”共产党，以此解决了内心的挣扎。“党就是我的家庭……她离我如此之近，每一天我都感觉到她的存在，我为她工作。我需要她，正如她需要我一样。” 1955年，在斯大林去世两年后，诗人叶夫根尼·叶夫图申科（Yevgeny Yevtushenko）重申了这一主题，但带着显而易见的修正。在一首写给女性的诗中，他写道：“世界上我有两种爱：革命和你。”他的爱是分裂的，不再是对社会和历史的排他性承诺。此外，诗人还请求他的两位爱人原谅他偶尔的不忠。

The subjectivizing thrust of Soviet ideology sprang in part from Marxism and its Romantic roots, but also in part from the mandate to be socially useful that had been a staple of Russian culture long before the revolution. To truly live meant to rise above selfish pursuits and devote one’s life to society and history, so as to remake accursed, backward Russia through the power of personal example and an unflinching orientation toward the future. This disposition was at work, in extreme but recognizable form, throughout the years of Soviet rule, and it found particularly strong expression in Stalin’s time. In the post-Stalin period its intensity waned. Writing in 1936, the brooding young Moscow worker and komsomolist Alexander Ulianov resolved his feeling of being torn between two girls by proclaiming his devotion to the real love of his life—the “dear” Communist party. “The party is my family . . . She is close, so close to me, and every day I sense her presence, I work for her. And I need her as much as she needs me.” In 1955, two years after Stalin’s death, the poet Yevgeny Yevtushenko took up the same theme, but with revealing modulations. In a poem addressed to a woman, he wrote: “I have two loves in the world: the revolution and you.” His was a divided love, no longer an exclusive commitment to society and history. Moreover, the poet asked both his lovers to forgive him for occasional infidelities.
